The spawning biology of the Queen scallop Aequipecten opercularis has been characterised across its European range, with reproductive output scaling strongly with female body size. Field surveys indicate that individual females release between three million and six million eggs per year [Ri = between three million and six million eggs per year] at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], a maximum reproductive capacity that is realised across the annual spawning cycle. This high fecundity is supported by the substantial asymptotic wet weight of adult specimens, which reaches 107 grams [Wwi = 107 grams] in fully grown, reproductively mature individuals. The energetic investment per gamete is reflected in the minute wet weight at birth, where newly spawned eggs, measuring approximately 68 micrometres in diameter, have an estimated mass of just 0.000000164 grams [Wwb = 0.000000164 grams]. This extremely small mass, which is among the lowest recorded for any pectinid species, necessitates a period of intensive planktotrophic feeding during the larval phase before settlement can occur.

Under stable thermal conditions typical of the species' habitat, such as at 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the larval development of Aequipecten opercularis proceeds through a predictable sequence of ontogenetic transitions. Following external fertilisation, the free-swimming veliger larva undergoes a period of planktotrophic growth before reaching morphological competence for metamorphosis. The time since birth at metamorphosis has been documented to range from 11 to 30 days (11-30 days)  under these conditions, with a central tendency near 20 days, reflecting the variability inherent in larval feeding success and hydrodynamic conditions at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This metamorphic event, marked by the loss of the velum and the onset of juvenile gill development, represents a critical bottleneck in the life cycle, as the post-larval bivalve must locate a suitable substratum and initiate benthic feeding. The completion of this larval-juvenile transition is a prerequisite for the subsequent phases of somatic growth and reproductive maturation.

Sexual maturation in the Queen scallop is a gradual process that occurs over an extended period following settlement. Under the same thermal regime of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], individuals attain puberty at approximately 365 days since birth [tp = approximately 365 days since birth], a duration that coincides with the first full annual cycle of growth and gametogenesis. This age at puberty corresponds to the onset of gonadal activity and the first detectable signs of gamete production within the developing gonad, although the initial spawning events may be less fecund than those of larger, older individuals. The investment in reproductive tissue at this stage is constrained by the need to allocate resources toward somatic growth, as the scallop has not yet reached its final asymptotic body mass. Comparative studies within the Pectinidae suggest that this timing of maturation is consistent with the moderate lifespan and relatively rapid growth trajectory characteristic of the genus Aequipecten.

The maximum recorded lifespan of Aequipecten opercularis has been documented through mark-recapture studies and shell growth increment analysis, with the oldest individuals reaching approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Field data indicate that this lifespan is attained at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], the average annual temperature of the scallop's preferred sublittoral habitats. The slow accumulation of shell material over this decadal scale permits individuals to reach a maximum shell height of up to 9 centimeters [Li = up to 9 centimeters] in many populations, although some anomalous records from particularly productive grounds suggest that exceptionally favourable conditions can yield specimens approaching 11 centimeters [Li = 11 centimeters]. This incremental growth pattern, coupled with periodic spawning events, defines the species' demographic strategy.

In controlled hatchery experiments conducted at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the embryonic phase leading to the hatching of the trochophore larva lasts approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days], a duration comparable to that reported for the congener Pecten maximus. This rapid embryonic development is followed by a short period of yolk absorption before the onset of planktotrophic feeding. The post-metamorphic juvenile, or spat, then commences filter-feeding on phytoplankton, initiating a phase of accelerated somatic growth that will ultimately lead to the attainment of adult body mass. The maximum daily reproduction rate, derived from the annual fecundity of up to six million eggs per year, corresponds to approximately 16,438 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 16,438 eggs per day] at 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. Available data indicate that such high fecundity over the species' decade-long lifespan results in a cumulative reproductive output exceeding tens of millions of eggs per individual, underscoring the substantial gametic investment typical of pectinid bivalves.
